options: A number identifying a running process
questions.correctAnswer: A number identifying a running process
questions.explanation:
A PID identifies a process during its lifetime.

Why: Tools use it to inspect or signal a specific running process.

Example: ps displays PIDs beside commands.

Student note: PIDs can be reused after old processes exit, so check what you are targeting.

study.title: PID
study.simple: A PID identifies a process during its lifetime.
steps: Tools use it to inspect or signal a specific running process.
study.pitfall: PIDs can be reused after old processes exit, so check what you are targeting.
study.remember: Tools use it to inspect or signal a specific running process.

keyTerms.meaning: A PID identifies a process during its lifetime.

whyCorrect: A PID is the numeric identifier the operating system assigns to a running process. Process-management tools use that number to distinguish one running instance from another, which is why 'a number identifying a running process' is correct.
notes: A process is a program that is currently executing, together with its runtime state and resources.
Commands such as ps show PIDs so you can inspect or signal the correct process.
A PID is not permanently tied to one program; the number may be reused after a process exits.

questions.text: Which tool offers a live view of processes and CPU/memory usage?
questions.explanation:
top refreshes a running view of process/resource usage.

Why: It is useful for finding a process that suddenly consumes CPU.

Example: Sort by CPU to spot a busy service.

Student note: ps provides a snapshot rather than a constantly refreshing view.

study.title: top
study.simple: top refreshes a running view of process/resource usage.
steps: It is useful for finding a process that suddenly consumes CPU.
study.example: Sort by CPU to spot a busy service.
study.pitfall: ps provides a snapshot rather than a constantly refreshing view.
study.remember: It is useful for finding a process that suddenly consumes CPU.

keyTerms.meaning: top refreshes a running view of process/resource usage.

whyCorrect: top continuously refreshes process information and system resource usage, so you can watch CPU and memory activity change in real time. That makes it the best answer when the question asks for a live view rather than a one-time snapshot.
notes: ps is mainly a snapshot of processes at the moment the command runs.
top can help identify a process consuming unusually high CPU or memory.
Interactive tools may allow sorting or filtering so the busiest processes are easier to see.

questions.text: When an application can shut down cleanly, which signal is normally preferable to start with?
questions.explanation:
SIGTERM requests termination and allows many programs to handle cleanup.

Why: SIGKILL cannot be caught by the application.

Example: kill -TERM 1234 asks the specified process to exit.

Student note: Confirm the PID first, and do not assume the program will obey TERM.

study.title: Clean termination
study.simple: SIGTERM requests termination and allows many programs to handle cleanup.
steps: SIGKILL cannot be caught by the application.
study.example: kill -TERM 1234 asks the specified process to exit.
study.pitfall: Confirm the PID first, and do not assume the program will obey TERM.
study.remember: SIGKILL cannot be caught by the application.

keyTerms.meaning: SIGTERM requests termination and allows many programs to handle cleanup.

whyCorrect: SIGTERM is a request for a process to terminate. Many applications can catch it and perform cleanup such as closing files or saving state before exiting. SIGKILL stops a process immediately and cannot be handled, so SIGTERM is normally the safer first choice.
notes: kill sends a signal; despite its name it does not always mean immediate forced termination.
SIGKILL is useful when a process will not respond, but it should not be the first option when clean shutdown matters.
Always confirm the PID before signalling a process.

questions.text: Which command displays current services on a systemd-based machine in more detail?
questions.explanation:
systemd-based Linux systems manage service units with systemctl.

Why: Status helps inspect whether a service is active or has failed.

Example: systemctl status nginx can report whether a web server runs.

Student note: Some distributions use service names that differ or another init system.

study.title: Service management
study.simple: systemd-based Linux systems manage service units with systemctl.
steps: Status helps inspect whether a service is active or has failed.
study.example: systemctl status nginx can report whether a web server runs.
study.pitfall: Some distributions use service names that differ or another init system.
study.remember: Status helps inspect whether a service is active or has failed.

keyTerms.meaning: systemd-based Linux systems manage service units with systemctl.

whyCorrect: On systemd-based systems, systemctl is the management command for service units. systemctl status service-name reports whether the unit is active, failed or inactive and usually includes recent diagnostic information, so it directly matches the request for service status.
notes: A service unit describes a background service managed by systemd.
systemctl start, stop and restart change service state; status mainly inspects it.
The exact unit name matters, for example nginx.service may be referred to as nginx.

questions.text: Why use journalctl -u nginx on a systemd-based host?
options: To inspect log entries for the nginx unit
questions.correctAnswer: To inspect log entries for the nginx unit
questions.explanation:
journalctl can query logs collected by systemd-journald.

Why: Filtering with -u focuses on a named service unit.

Example: journalctl -u nginx --since today narrows the investigation.

Student note: Some applications also write separate logs; look for a useful error and time window.

study.title: Service logs
study.simple: journalctl can query logs collected by systemd-journald.
steps: Filtering with -u focuses on a named service unit.
study.example: journalctl -u nginx --since today narrows the investigation.
study.pitfall: Some applications also write separate logs; look for a useful error and time window.
study.remember: Filtering with -u focuses on a named service unit.

keyTerms.meaning: journalctl can query logs collected by systemd-journald.

whyCorrect: journalctl reads logs collected by systemd-journald, and the -u option filters those logs to one systemd unit. Therefore journalctl -u nginx is specifically useful for seeing messages related to the nginx service.
notes: Service logs often explain why a unit failed even when systemctl status only gives a short summary.
Time filters such as --since today can narrow a large log.
Some applications also maintain their own log files, so journald is not always the only source of evidence.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the cron scheduling system?
options: Run specified jobs according to time rules
questions.correctAnswer: Run specified jobs according to time rules
questions.explanation:
A cron job describes a command and when it should run.

Why: It is useful for repeated unattended tasks.

Example: A nightly backup script can have a cron entry.

Student note: Test a script's PATH and permissions because cron's environment differs from an interactive shell.

study.title: cron
study.simple: A cron job describes a command and when it should run.
steps: It is useful for repeated unattended tasks.
study.example: A nightly backup script can have a cron entry.
study.pitfall: Test a script's PATH and permissions because cron's environment differs from an interactive shell.
study.remember: It is useful for repeated unattended tasks.

keyTerms.meaning: A cron job describes a command and when it should run.

whyCorrect: cron is designed to run commands automatically according to time-based schedules. A cron entry combines timing fields with a command, which is why 'run specified jobs according to time rules' is the correct description.
notes: Cron is useful for repeated jobs such as backups, cleanup and report generation.
A cron job may run with a smaller environment than your interactive shell, so PATH and permissions can matter.
Scheduling a job is not enough; you should also monitor whether the job actually succeeds.

questions.text: Which command reports active swap areas?
questions.explanation:
Swap is disk-backed backing space available to the memory manager.

Why: swapon --show lists active areas.

Example: free -h also shows a summary of swap use.

Student note: Do not disable swap on a pressured system without understanding the consequences.

study.title: Swap reporting
study.simple: Swap is disk-backed backing space available to the memory manager.
steps: swapon --show lists active areas.
study.example: free -h also shows a summary of swap use.
study.pitfall: Do not disable swap on a pressured system without understanding the consequences.

keyTerms.meaning: Swap is disk-backed backing space available to the memory manager.

whyCorrect: Swap provides disk-backed space the memory manager can use when appropriate, and swapon --show lists the swap areas currently enabled. That is why it directly answers a question asking which command reports active swap.
notes: free -h shows a summary of RAM and swap usage but does not replace detailed swap-area information.
Swap is much slower than RAM, so heavy swapping can indicate memory pressure.
Changing swap configuration on a live system should be done carefully.

questions.text: What is one important difference between df and du?
options: df reports filesystem space; du totals storage used by selected paths
df changes permissions; du changes owner
questions.correctAnswer: df reports filesystem space; du totals storage used by selected paths
questions.explanation:
The tools answer different disk-usage questions.

Why: df checks space on a filesystem, whereas du investigates directories and files.

Example: A filesystem can show full in df, then du can help identify large paths.

Student note: Deleted-but-still-open files can make these reports differ temporarily.

study.title: df versus du
study.simple: The tools answer different disk-usage questions.
steps: df checks space on a filesystem, whereas du investigates directories and files.
study.example: A filesystem can show full in df, then du can help identify large paths.
study.pitfall: Deleted-but-still-open files can make these reports differ temporarily.
study.remember: df checks space on a filesystem, whereas du investigates directories and files.

keyTerms.meaning: The tools answer different disk-usage questions.

whyCorrect: df reports space usage at the filesystem level, such as total, used and available space. du walks selected files or directories and totals the storage they consume. The correct option identifies this different scope.
notes: Use df when asking 'which filesystem is full?' and du when asking 'which files or folders are using the space?'.
The numbers can differ because of filesystem overhead, permissions and deleted files that are still open.
df -h and du -h use human-readable sizes.

questions.text: Which command shows block devices with filesystem identifiers useful for mounting?
questions.explanation:
lsblk -f lists block devices and known filesystem metadata.

Why: It helps confirm the partition and UUID before editing mount settings.

Example: Check /dev/sdb1's filesystem type before attempting to mount it.

Student note: Do not guess disk device names on a live machine.

study.title: lsblk -f
study.simple: lsblk -f lists block devices and known filesystem metadata.
steps: It helps confirm the partition and UUID before editing mount settings.
study.example: Check /dev/sdb1's filesystem type before attempting to mount it.
study.pitfall: Do not guess disk device names on a live machine.
study.remember: It helps confirm the partition and UUID before editing mount settings.

keyTerms.meaning: lsblk -f lists block devices and known filesystem metadata.

whyCorrect: lsblk lists block devices, and the -f option adds filesystem information such as filesystem type, label and UUID. Those identifiers are exactly the details an administrator often needs before mounting or editing /etc/fstab.
notes: Block devices include disks and partitions such as /dev/sda and /dev/sda1.
The UUID identifies a filesystem independently of a changing /dev/sdX order.
Confirm device identity before making destructive storage changes.

questions.text: Why may an administrator put a UUID rather than a /dev/sdX name in /etc/fstab?
options: UUIDs are generally less sensitive to device-name order changing between boots
It makes data impossible to delete
questions.correctAnswer: UUIDs are generally less sensitive to device-name order changing between boots
questions.explanation:
/etc/fstab can use a filesystem UUID as a stable reference.

Why: Device enumeration such as /dev/sdb can change when disks are added or reordered.

Example: Use blkid to find a UUID before drafting a mount entry.

Student note: A wrong fstab entry can disrupt boot, so validate it safely.

study.title: UUID mounting
study.simple: /etc/fstab can use a filesystem UUID as a stable reference.
steps: Device enumeration such as /dev/sdb can change when disks are added or reordered.
study.example: Use blkid to find a UUID before drafting a mount entry.
study.pitfall: A wrong fstab entry can disrupt boot, so validate it safely.
study.remember: Device enumeration such as /dev/sdb can change when disks are added or reordered.

keyTerms.meaning: /etc/fstab can use a filesystem UUID as a stable reference.

whyCorrect: Device names such as /dev/sdb can change when hardware is added or discovered in a different order. A filesystem UUID is stored with the filesystem and is therefore usually a more stable reference for /etc/fstab across reboots.
notes: blkid and lsblk -f can display filesystem UUIDs.
A wrong UUID or malformed fstab entry can cause mount failures and may affect boot.
UUID stability is about identifying the filesystem, not guaranteeing the device itself is healthy.

questions.text: What is the main benefit of the directory setgid bit on a collaborative folder?
options: New entries normally inherit the parent directory's group
It gives every user full root privileges
questions.correctAnswer: New entries normally inherit the parent directory's group
questions.explanation:
Shared group inheritance helps files created by different team members remain in a useful group.

Why: A directory with setgid passes its group to new entries in common Linux filesystems.

Example: chmod g+s /srv/team can support collaborative ownership.

Student note: Group inheritance alone does not guarantee write access; check mode bits/default ACL.

study.title: Directory setgid
study.simple: Shared group inheritance helps files created by different team members remain in a useful group.
steps: A directory with setgid passes its group to new entries in common Linux filesystems.
study.example: chmod g+s /srv/team can support collaborative ownership.
study.pitfall: Group inheritance alone does not guarantee write access; check mode bits/default ACL.
study.remember: A directory with setgid passes its group to new entries in common Linux filesystems.

keyTerms.meaning: Shared group inheritance helps files created by different team members remain in a useful group.

whyCorrect: The setgid bit on a directory causes newly created entries to inherit that directory's group on common Linux filesystems. This keeps collaborative files in the shared team group instead of switching to each creator's primary group.
notes: setgid helps with group ownership inheritance but does not itself grant all required permissions.
Default ACLs can be combined with setgid to control the permissions new entries receive.
chmod g+s directory sets the directory setgid bit.

questions.text: What does an ACL allow beyond the traditional owner/group/other permissions?
options: Rights for additional named users or groups
questions.correctAnswer: Rights for additional named users or groups
questions.explanation:
Access control lists provide finer-grained permission entries.

Why: For example, one named user can receive access without opening permissions to all others.

Example: getfacl and setfacl inspect and change common POSIX ACLs.

Student note: The ACL mask may limit the effective rights of named entries.

study.title: ACL
study.simple: Access control lists provide finer-grained permission entries.
steps: For example, one named user can receive access without opening permissions to all others.
study.example: getfacl and setfacl inspect and change common POSIX ACLs.
study.pitfall: The ACL mask may limit the effective rights of named entries.
study.remember: For example, one named user can receive access without opening permissions to all others.

keyTerms.meaning: Access control lists provide finer-grained permission entries.

whyCorrect: Traditional mode bits only describe owner, group and others. An ACL can add entries for extra named users or groups, giving finer-grained access without changing the basic owner/group model. That is why the correct answer focuses on additional named identities.
notes: getfacl displays ACL entries; setfacl changes them on systems that support POSIX ACLs.
The ACL mask can limit the effective permissions of named users and groups.
A trailing + in an ls -l permission display often indicates extended ACL information.

questions.text: Which command normally applies the mode rwxr-x--- to a directory?
questions.explanation:
Numeric mode 750 gives owner 7=rwx, group 5=r-x, others 0=---.

Why: It lets group members traverse/read the directory but not edit its entries.

Example: chmod 750 /srv/reports sets these mode bits.

Student note: To list/traverse a directory correctly, understand read and execute separately.

study.title: chmod 750
study.simple: Numeric mode 750 gives owner 7=rwx, group 5=r-x, others 0=---.
steps: It lets group members traverse/read the directory but not edit its entries.
study.pitfall: To list/traverse a directory correctly, understand read and execute separately.
study.remember: It lets group members traverse/read the directory but not edit its entries.

keyTerms.meaning: Numeric mode 750 gives owner 7=rwx, group 5=r-x, others 0=---.

whyCorrect: Permission digits are calculated with read=4, write=2 and execute=1. In 750, owner gets 7=rwx, group gets 5=r-x and others get 0=---, which is exactly the requested rwxr-x--- mode.
notes: Read the digits in owner-group-others order.
On a directory, execute means traversal and write controls creating/removing directory entries when other required permissions are present.
chmod changes permissions, not ownership.

questions.text: Which command is commonly used to see an account's UID and group memberships?
questions.explanation:
Linux has user IDs and group IDs for access decisions.

Why: id prints identity and supplementary group information.

Example: id thandi helps confirm group membership after account changes.

Student note: After modifying groups, an old login session may not reflect new membership.

study.title: id command
study.simple: Linux has user IDs and group IDs for access decisions.
steps: id prints identity and supplementary group information.
study.example: id thandi helps confirm group membership after account changes.
study.pitfall: After modifying groups, an old login session may not reflect new membership.
study.remember: id prints identity and supplementary group information.

keyTerms.meaning: Linux has user IDs and group IDs for access decisions.

whyCorrect: The id command asks the system for account identity information. id username shows the user's UID, primary GID and supplementary groups, which is why it is the right tool for checking group membership.
notes: Linux access decisions are based on numeric UIDs and GIDs even though commands usually display names.
Supplementary groups give a user membership in additional groups beyond the primary group.
A newly changed group membership may require a fresh login session before it appears in that process environment.

questions.text: Which statement is most accurate about a backup?
options: A backup needs independent safe storage and a tested recovery procedure
An archive on the same failing disk is always enough
A successful command guarantees future recovery
Backups only matter for source code
questions.correctAnswer: A backup needs independent safe storage and a tested recovery procedure
questions.explanation:
A backup should survive expected failure scenarios and be restorable.

Why: Testing recovery validates that data and procedures are useful.

Example: Store a copy outside the primary machine and practise restoring selected files.

Student note: tar can create archives; it does not by itself establish a complete backup strategy.

study.title: Backups
study.simple: A backup should survive expected failure scenarios and be restorable.
steps: Testing recovery validates that data and procedures are useful.
study.example: Store a copy outside the primary machine and practise restoring selected files.
study.pitfall: tar can create archives; it does not by itself establish a complete backup strategy.
study.remember: Testing recovery validates that data and procedures are useful.

keyTerms.meaning: A backup should survive expected failure scenarios and be restorable.

whyCorrect: A useful backup must survive the failure it is meant to protect against and must be restorable. Keeping an independent safe copy and testing recovery proves those two properties, whereas merely creating an archive does not guarantee either one.
notes: A backup on the same failing disk may disappear with the original data.
Restore testing checks both the backup data and the recovery procedure.
Retention, access control and off-site/off-system copies are part of a real backup strategy.

questions.text: A server receives an IP address automatically during network startup. Which service commonly provides that configuration?
questions.explanation:
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol commonly provides network settings to clients.

Why: It may supply IP address, gateway, DNS and—in some PXE settings—boot-related information.

Example: A machine obtains network parameters when joining a managed LAN.

Student note: PXE is a network-boot workflow, not a replacement for DHCP itself.

study.title: DHCP
study.simple: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol commonly provides network settings to clients.
steps: It may supply IP address, gateway, DNS and—in some PXE settings—boot-related information.
study.example: A machine obtains network parameters when joining a managed LAN.
study.pitfall: PXE is a network-boot workflow, not a replacement for DHCP itself.
study.remember: It may supply IP address, gateway, DNS and—in some PXE settings—boot-related information.

keyTerms.meaning: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol commonly provides network settings to clients.

whyCorrect: DHCP is the protocol commonly used to automatically provide network configuration to a client when it joins a network. It can supply an IP address, subnet information, default gateway and DNS settings, so it matches the scenario.
notes: DHCP reduces the need to configure each client manually.
PXE boot environments often rely on DHCP for network and boot-related information, but DHCP and PXE are not the same thing.
The client usually leases the address for a period rather than owning it permanently.

questions.text: Scenario: After a server reboot, a shared service does not start and staff cannot access a mounted data volume. Outline a safe fault-finding order, including evidence collection and recovery checks.
questions.correctAnswer: Check service status with systemctl and relevant logs with journalctl; inspect mount state with findmnt/mount, block identifiers with lsblk -f or blkid, and available disk/inodes with df -h/df -i; compare /etc/fstab entries with current UUIDs; check permissions; make a backed-up correction, test mount -a where appropriate, restart only after the underlying issue is resolved, and verify service/client access.
aiRubric: Checks actual mounted devices and UUID/fstab consistency
questions.aiReferenceNotes: A service may fail because its data filesystem did not mount or is inaccessible. Record the exact service error and when it began. Verify the device, mount state, capacity and permissions. Correct one known cause at a time and check both mount and service. A stale UUID in fstab could leave /srv/data unmounted, causing the service to fail. Do not format a disk or use chmod 777 as a first troubleshooting step.
questions.explanation:
A service may fail because its data filesystem did not mount or is inaccessible.

Method:
1. Record the exact service error and when it began.
2. Verify the device, mount state, capacity and permissions.
3. Correct one known cause at a time and check both mount and service.

Example: A stale UUID in fstab could leave /srv/data unmounted, causing the service to fail.

Student note: Do not format a disk or use chmod 777 as a first troubleshooting step.

study.title: Post-reboot troubleshooting
study.simple: A service may fail because its data filesystem did not mount or is inaccessible.
study.stepsTitle: How to work through this scenario
steps: Record the exact service error and when it began.
Verify the device, mount state, capacity and permissions.
Correct one known cause at a time and check both mount and service.
study.example: A stale UUID in fstab could leave /srv/data unmounted, causing the service to fail.
study.pitfall: Do not format a disk or use chmod 777 as a first troubleshooting step.
study.remember: Record the exact service error and when it began.

keyTerms.meaning: A service may fail because its data filesystem did not mount or is inaccessible.

whyCorrect: The service depends on its data volume, so troubleshooting should start by collecting evidence from the service and logs, then verifying the storage dependency before changing anything. Checking mounts, device identifiers, capacity, fstab and permissions follows that dependency chain and avoids risky guesswork.
notes: Troubleshoot from evidence: record the exact error before restarting or changing configuration.
A stale UUID or failed mount can make a service appear broken even though the service software itself is fine.
After fixing the root cause, verify both the mount and the client-facing service; one successful command is not enough proof.

questions.text: Scenario: A company needs nightly backups of a Linux project directory. Design a simple scheduling and recovery plan using standard tools, including how you would know backups really work.
questions.correctAnswer: Choose data scope and frequency, produce dated backups (for example tar or suitable incremental tool), use cron/systemd timers with controlled permissions and logging, store a protected copy off the source disk, monitor for failure, define retention, periodically restore sample files in a safe location, compare expected content and document recovery steps.
aiRubric: Includes secure separate storage and retention
questions.aiReferenceNotes: A backup is valuable only when it can be recovered within the required time. Decide what data is essential and how often it changes. Schedule, protect and record each backup result. Perform and document regular restore tests. A job can use tar to archive /srv/project to a separate destination, followed by a periodic test restore. A green cron exit code alone does not prove that all important files can be restored.
questions.explanation:
A backup is valuable only when it can be recovered within the required time.

Method:
1. Decide what data is essential and how often it changes.
2. Schedule, protect and record each backup result.
3. Perform and document regular restore tests.

Example: A job can use tar to archive /srv/project to a separate destination, followed by a periodic test restore.

Student note: A green cron exit code alone does not prove that all important files can be restored.

study.title: Backup and restore workflow
study.simple: A backup is valuable only when it can be recovered within the required time.
study.stepsTitle: How to work through this scenario
steps: Decide what data is essential and how often it changes.
Schedule, protect and record each backup result.
Perform and document regular restore tests.
study.example: A job can use tar to archive /srv/project to a separate destination, followed by a periodic test restore.
study.pitfall: A green cron exit code alone does not prove that all important files can be restored.
study.remember: Decide what data is essential and how often it changes.

keyTerms.meaning: A backup is valuable only when it can be recovered within the required time.

whyCorrect: A complete backup solution needs more than a scheduled archive command. The answer covers scope, schedule, protected storage, logging, retention and actual restore tests, which together show that the organisation can recover the project data rather than merely create backup files.
notes: Decide recovery needs first: what must be restored, how much data loss is acceptable and how quickly recovery is required.
Automated jobs should produce logs or alerts so silent failures are noticed.
Regular sample restores are the practical proof that backups are usable.
